_about: Terms explained by a popover on first use in each blog post. Edit here and rebuild the blog. Fields: term (label), match (regular expression, matched on word boundaries), case (true = case-sensitive), note (plain English, one or two sentences), url (null = popover only), src (name of the outside source), series (optional: only mark in these series).

terms.note: AI that combines a learning system, such as a language model, with explicit symbols and rules a machine can check, so each covers the other's weaknesses.
A formal, shared definition of the things in a domain (such as supplier or corporate group), their properties and how they relate, written so that software can reason with it.
Facts stored as a network of things and the named relationships between them, rather than as rows in tables.
One fact written as subject, predicate and object, such as ‘Supplier A · belongs to · Group X’. It is the basic unit of RDF.
Resource Description Framework: the W3C standard for writing data as triples, so that data from different systems can be linked.
Web Ontology Language: the W3C standard for writing an ontology so that a reasoner can draw conclusions from it and detect contradictions.
Shapes Constraint Language: the W3C standard for checking that data meets stated rules, and reporting exactly which rule each record breaks.
The W3C query language for RDF data: roughly what SQL is to tables.
A family of formal logics designed for describing categories and their relationships, on which OWL is built.
A statement is entailed by some facts when it must be true whenever those facts are true; a reasoner works out what is entailed.
Translating ordinary language into a formal representation of its meaning that a machine can check or execute.
Planning Domain Definition Language: a standard way to describe states, actions and their preconditions so that an automated planner can search for a plan.
A way of writing a problem as facts and rules, for which a solver searches for every consistent set of conclusions.
Software that derives what logically follows from stated facts and rules, and finds where they contradict each other.
In ontology work: the smallest set of statements that together produce a conclusion or a contradiction. Remove any one and the conclusion no longer follows.
Adding up the probabilities of every possible world that satisfies the rules. It gives the probability that a model's beliefs obey the rules.
When a model satisfies the rules for the wrong reasons: the output passes every check, but the model has misread the world.
A statistical model that learns a smooth relationship from data and also says how uncertain it is at each point.
An open-source Python library for building AI agents as a graph of steps, with state passed from step to step.
An AI system trained on very large amounts of text to predict and generate language. It reads and writes fluently, but does not check its output against rules on its own.
When an AI model states something false or invented as if it were fact.
Further training an existing model on a smaller, specific set of examples to adapt it to a task.
Giving a language model relevant documents found at question time, so it answers from them rather than from memory alone.
The system that holds the authoritative version of a piece of business data, such as the ERP for purchase orders.
Give each person or system only the access its task needs, and nothing more.
Splitting a process so that no one person can carry it out end to end, for example creating a supplier and paying it.
An open standard that lets one system act on a user's behalf in another with a limited token, without sharing the user's password.
Trading one access token for another, for example one that records both the user and the agent acting for them. Standardised for OAuth 2.0 in RFC 8693.
Putting a draft or pending layer between an agent's action and the real record, so nothing takes effect until it is explicitly promoted.
Limiting a tool an agent needs to the operations and targets the task warrants, such as ‘create drafts for this supplier only’.
Undoing an action's effect with a new, opposite action, such as a cancellation or credit note, because the original cannot simply be erased.
An operation is idempotent if running it twice has the same effect as running it once, so a retry cannot create a duplicate.
Hiding instructions in content an AI model reads, such as an email or web page, so that the model follows them as if the user had asked.
Testing a system by deliberately attacking it as an adversary would, to find weaknesses before others do.
A structured argument, backed by evidence, that a system is acceptably safe for a particular use.
A single score from 0 to 1 that balances how many flagged cases were right (precision) with how many real cases were found (recall).
A benchmark of real software issues from open-source projects, used to test whether AI agents can fix code.
A mechanism that stops further actions automatically once a limit is crossed, such as a number of failures or a total value.
Several independent layers of protection, so that a failure in one is caught by another.
An open standard for connecting AI assistants to outside tools and data, so one connection works across many assistants.
Working out which records in different systems refer to the same real thing, such as one customer appearing in email, chat and the CRM.
If a check cannot be made, for example because a service is down, the action is refused rather than allowed.
